en: seal the pot and cook slowly

does: Layers marinated meat and nearly cooked rice in a heavy pot, closes the lid tightly, often with a rope of dough, and finishes the dish in its own steam over a very low heat. Nothing is stirred, and the pot is opened at the table.

intro.what: Layered rice and marinated meat finish in a tightly sealed pot over restrained heat.
intro.why: Dum depends on contained steam and intact layers. Keeping the pot closed matters more than repeated checking or stirring.

how: Spread the marinated meat in an even layer on the bottom of a heavy pot, with a little ghee.
Pile the nearly cooked rice over the meat in loose layers, with herbs, crisp fried onions and ghee between them. Do not press it down.
Sprinkle saffron steeped in warm milk over the top.
Seal the gap between the lid and the pot with a rope of firm dough, pressing it in all round. A heavy cloth under the lid works too.
Set the pot on a flat plate of iron over a medium heat for a short spell to build up steam, then turn the heat to its lowest and leave it undisturbed.
Rest the sealed pot off the heat before it is broken open. Fold the rice and the meat together from the bottom with a flat spoon, so the layers are kept.

cues.text: A rich scent of spice, saffron and ghee seeps out from under the lid when the pot is nearly ready.
A faint, steady hiss comes from the pot, with no hard bubbling.
The grains of rice on top are long, dry and separate, and the meat below is tender and coated in a thick gravy.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the seal leak, so that the steam escapes and the rice on top stays hard.
mistakes.fix: Press the rope of dough into the join all round, and patch any gap at once.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping the heat too high, so that the bottom layer scorches.
mistakes.fix: Set the pot on a flat iron plate and turn the heat to its lowest once the steam builds.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the lid to look, which lets the steam out and breaks the slow cooking.
mistakes.fix: Leave the pot shut until the end of the rest.

mistakes.mistake: Stirring the layers together, so that the dish turns into a heap of mush.
mistakes.fix: Dig down to the bottom with a flat spoon and lift the layers out whole.

quiz.question: Why seal the lid closely for this dum method?
choices: To retain the steam that finishes the layered dish.
To dry the upper rice with escaping steam.
To make stirring through the layers easier.
quiz.because: The seal contains the moisture on which the undisturbed cooking depends.

quiz.question: How should rice be placed over the meat?
choices: Packed firmly into a dense block.
In loose layers without pressing it down.
Stirred into the meat before sealing.
quiz.because: Loose layering preserves the structure rather than compressing or mixing the grains.

quiz.question: What sound fits the intended gentle cooking?
choices: A sharp crackle from a drying base.
quiz.because: The quiet hiss accompanies the restrained heat used after steam builds.

quiz.question: The base scorches while the pot stays sealed. What should change?
choices: Reduce the heat and use the iron plate beneath the pot.
Increase the direct flame under the base.
Press the layers tightly against the bottom.
quiz.because: The plate and lower heat moderate the heat reaching the bottom layer.

comes_after.why: The rice goes into the pot only nearly cooked, so a cook has to be able to stop it at that point first.
The meat goes into the pot already marinated, and cooks in the steam without being browned.

variant_of.differs: The seal is for a pot on the stove, over a very low heat, and not for a long bake. The food is layered, half-cooked rice over marinated meat, and cooks in the steam and scent held in the pot, never stirred.
A pilaf cooks raw rice in a measured amount of stock. Here the rice is boiled nearly done first, laid over meat that has not been browned, and finished by steam alone.
